May display: name, year of establishment, addresses and contacts; nature of services (pull); partners' names, qualifications, experience (pull); employees (pull); job vacancies incl. articleship; number of articled assistants (pull); nature of assignments handled (pull); passport-style photographs; articles, professional updates, bulletin boards, educational videos; chat rooms (with confidentiality); document management with client login; link to firm's social networking page (but don't solicit visits or likes); online advice to clients who request it (free or paid); links to ICAI, government, regulators, other professional bodies.

Not allowed: client names and fees (except as required by a regulator, with the italicised disclosure note naming the regulator and rule); banner or other advertisements; content unbecoming of a CA; information at material variance from ICAI records.
No restriction on colours used.
Website address as near as possible to the member/firm name; not solicitation; ESB decides difficulties.
Keep client matters secret.
P.upd: Exam position (SM): pull only. The Code of Ethics 2026 allows push technology for services not exclusive to CAs, but this is not in the Nov 2026 RTP amendments.

P.g: I. Self-regulatory measures and fee dependence
P.label: Self-regulatory; fee dependence
P.title: Recommended self-regulatory measures and fee dependence
P.short: Recommended self-regulatory measures and fee dependence
P.law: Recommendatory measures for equitable flow of work; Council expects compliance in spirit.
notes: Branch audits: statutory auditors with 10 or more members should not do branch audits; local firms with fewer than 10 members should — except where branch records are kept at HO or significant operations are at the branch.
Joint audit: for large companies encourage associating a firm with fewer than 5 members; senior firm should not object.
Staff ratio: at least 1 member for every 5 non-qualified staff engaged in professional work (excluding articled/audit assistants, typists, peons).
Disclosure of interest: auditors should disclose payments received for other services through other firms in which they are partner/proprietor.
Recommended minimum scale of fees for Class A, B and C cities.

Fee dependence (relative size): disclose to the Institute where, for two consecutive years, gross annual fees from one audit client exceed 40% of the firm's total fees (non-PIE) or 20% (PIE). Exempt if the firm's total fees do not exceed ₹20 lakh, and for audits of government companies, public undertakings, nationalised banks, public financial institutions, regulators, or appointments made by Government. Threat: self-interest and intimidation.
PIE: listed entity; entity defined as PIE by law; entity whose audit law requires to follow listed-entity independence; banks and insurance companies.
P.upd: Beyond the Nov 2026 syllabus (not in RTP): the 2026 Code introduced revised requirements for reporting fee-related disclosures to the Institute (ESB announcement), a chapter on minimum professional fees (exposure draft), provisions on non-payment of audit fees, and an advisory to accept audit fees only through digital payments/banking channels. Vol II also follows IESBA 2024 fee provisions for PIEs (e.g., 15% fee-dependence disclosure to TCWG). Check the BoS note for which of these ICAI has made examinable.

P.g: I. Self-regulatory measures and fee dependence
P.label: Nov 2026 amendments
P.title: What's examinable for Nov 2026 — confirmed by the RTP
P.law: The Nov 2026 RTP (Part I, Chapter 19) lists exactly three amendments to Professional Ethics. Everything else is as per your study material.
notes: 1. FS Part I Clause (9) wording: 'sections 139 to 141 of the Companies Act, 2013 or any other law pertaining to appointment of auditors' (FS I(9)).
2. SS Part II Clause (5) inserted: acting as auditor of a company in contravention of the Companies Act, 2013 (SS II(5)).

3. Tax audit limit (replaces SM Chapter VI): 60 per member per financial year, aggregate of individual and firm capacity, cannot be shared among partners, excludes s.44AD/44ADA/44AE audits, revised reports not counted (GL: Tax audit limit). SM Illustration 37's answer becomes guilty.

Not in the RTP, so keep SM figures: company audit ceiling 30 (GL: Company audit limit); teaching 25 hours a week (FS I(11)); goodwill sale within 1 year (FS I(2)); websites pull-only (Adv: Website); educational-video rule (FS I(6)); write-up conditions (Adv: Write-up); non-audit fee trigger ₹50 crore (GL: Non-audit fee ceiling); indebtedness ₹1 lakh (GL: Indebtedness).

Code of Ethics 2026 (applicable 1 April 2026) changed several of those numbers (40 audits, 35 hours, 3 years, push for non-exclusive services, new MCS items). They are current practice but outside your exam cut-off; at most, add one line after an SM-based answer.
The RTP's ethics questions are in the RTP Nov 2026 section of the question bank.

Q.q: A CA in practice was suspended for 6 months and surrendered his COP. During suspension he took no audits but appeared before income-tax authorities as a representative in his capacity as a CA.
Q.a:
Provision: Section 6 — no member shall practise without a COP. Council's view (A.C. Kaher): once a person becomes a member he is bound by the Act and Regulations; a suspended member cannot practise in any other capacity separable from his capacity as a member.

Analysis: Tax representation is practice (s.2(2), Reg 191). He appeared before tax authorities only because he is a CA. Suspension from practice covers every form of practice.

Conclusion: He cannot represent before tax authorities during suspension. Guilty of professional misconduct (contravention of the Act → SS Part II(1)).
Q.trap: Don't argue 'he did no audit'. Any practice during suspension is barred.

Q.q: Mr. A, a CA in practice, agreed to select and recruit personnel and conduct training programmes for a client to whom he provides no assurance service.
Q.a:
Provision: s.2(2)(iv) — Council's resolution permits the full range of Management Consultancy and other Services, which includes personnel recruitment and selection, and development of human resources including design and conduct of training programmes, work study, job description and evaluation.

Analysis: Both activities are listed MCS items. No assurance relationship exists, so no independence issue under s.144 Companies Act.

Conclusion: Mr. A is not guilty.

Q.q: X and Y, partners of a CA firm, are in charge of the head office and a branch 80 km from municipal limits respectively. They put up the firm's name board at both offices and also at their respective residences.
Q.a:
Provision: Council decision under s.27 — a name board may be put up at a member's residence with designation CA only if it is the name plate/board of the individual member, not of the firm.

Analysis: Each office has a separate member in charge, so s.27 is complied with and the 80 km distance is irrelevant. The problem is the firm's name board at residences.

Conclusion: X and Y are guilty of misconduct for displaying the firm's name board at their residences.
Q.trap: Distance is a red herring — each office already has a partner in charge.

Q.q: Mr. K, a sole proprietor with an office in a Chennai suburb, opens a second office within the city near the income-tax office, 30 km away, and employs a retired Income-tax Commissioner (non-CA) to run it.
Q.a:
Provision: s.27 — each office must be in separate charge of a member, but one member may be in charge of two offices if the second is in the same premises, the same city, or within 50 km of the municipal limits of the city of the first office.

Analysis: The second office is in the same city, within the exemption. The retired Commissioner can be employed but cannot be 'in charge' as he is not a member; Mr. K himself must be in charge of both.

Conclusion: No misconduct if Mr. K is in charge of both offices; he must declare which is the main office.
Q.trap: If the question says the non-CA is 'in charge', the answer flips to guilty.

Q.q: CA C allowed his brother-in-law P (not a CA) to practise in the name of CA C. He also allowed CA T, an employee of his firm, to practise in his name.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (1) — guilty if he allows any person to practise in his name as a CA unless that person is also a CA in practice and is his partner or employee.

Analysis: P is not a CA → not permitted. CA T is a CA employed by him → permitted.

Conclusion: CA C is guilty under Clause (1) for allowing P; no misconduct regarding CA T.

Q.q: Mr. Qureshi, a CA proprietor, died in an accident. His widow proposes to sell his practice to CA Pardeshi for ₹5 lakh, including the right to use the name 'Qureshi and Associates'. Can she, and can Pardeshi practise in that name as proprietor?
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (2) read with Council resolution — goodwill of a deceased proprietor's firm may be sold/transferred to an eligible member; legal heir must seek the Institute's permission within the prescribed time; consideration not contingent on future profits.

Analysis: Selling the practice for a fixed ₹5 lakh is a sale of goodwill, not fee sharing.

Conclusion: Permissible; Pardeshi can practise in that firm name as proprietor, subject to ICAI approval within the time limit.
Q.trap: Exam figure: permission within 1 year of death (SM; not changed by the Nov 2026 RTP). ICAI later extended it to 3 years — add as one line only.

Q.q: Mr. S, a CA in practice, published a book giving his personal details as author, including his professional experience.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (6) — soliciting directly or indirectly; Council: in a book/article a member may state the designation CA and firm name but not professional attainments.

Analysis: Describing professional experience in detail is indirect advertisement of attainments.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (6).

Q.q: M/s XYZ created a website containing firm details, partners' bio-data and passport-size photographs of all partners.
Q.a:
Provision: Website guidelines under FS Part I Clause (6) — any format, pull model, must not solicit; firm details, partners' bio-data and passport-style photographs are permitted.

Conclusion: No violation, assuming the site runs on pull and shows no client names or fees.

Q.q: M/s LMN responded to a State Government tender for computerisation of land revenue records and paid ₹50,000 as earnest money.
Q.a:
Provision: Proviso to FS Part I Clause (6) and tender guidelines — members may respond to tenders; the bar is only for areas exclusively reserved for CAs (audit, attestation) without a prescribed minimum fee. Reasonable EMD is allowed; exorbitant EMD may be examined by ESB.

Analysis: Computerisation of records is not an exclusive CA area; ₹50,000 EMD is reasonable.

Conclusion: Not guilty.

Q.q: Mr. Honest wrote letters to two CA firms requesting them to allot him professional work. Another CA reported this to ICAI.
Q.a:
Provision: Proviso (i) to FS Part I Clause (6) — nothing prevents a CA from applying, requesting, inviting or securing work from another CA in practice.

Conclusion: Not guilty.

Q.q: A practising CA uses a visiting card designating himself 'Chartered Accountant' and 'Tax Consultant'.
Q.a:
Provision: s.7 read with FS Part I Clause (7) — no designation other than CA on visiting cards unless a university degree or membership of a body recognised by the Central Government or Council.

Analysis: 'Tax Consultant' is neither.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (7).

Q.q: B, a CA in practice, is a partner in 3 firms and prints the names of all three firms on his personal letterhead.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (7) prohibits advertising attainments (and, per Council, the date of setting up practice on letterheads) but there is no bar on printing names of all firms in which a COP-holding member is partner.

Conclusion: Not guilty.

Q.q: The offer document of a listed company mentions its director, Mr. D (CA in practice), with his professional attainments and specialisations.
Q.a:
Provision: Council communication under FS Part I Clauses (6) and (7) — the member must ensure that prospectus or announcements do not describe his expertise or specialisation; only 'Chartered Accountant' and other directorships may be mentioned, not his firm.

Conclusion: Mr. D is guilty under Clauses (6) and (7). He should have asked the company to have such material approved by him.

Q.q: A CA in practice empanelled as an Insolvency Professional mentions 'Insolvency Professional' on his visiting cards and letterheads. A neighbour complains.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (7) allows titles recognised by the Central Government or Council. The Council permits 'Insolvency Professional' and 'Registered Valuer' on visiting cards and letterheads.

Conclusion: Not guilty; the complaint fails.

Q.q: Mr. X accepted a tax audit under s.44AB and started work within two days because the client was in a hurry. Realising his mistake, he sent a registered letter to the previous tax auditor before signing the report.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (8) — must communicate in writing with the previous auditor before accepting the position. Applies to all audits including tax audit.

Analysis: Communication after acceptance and commencement defeats the purpose (to learn of professional reasons not to accept).

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (8).
Q.trap: The 'conditional acceptance' relief is only for government/bank audits with tight timelines — not a private client in a hurry.

Q.q: W sent a letter under certificate of posting to the previous auditor before starting the audit.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (8); J.S. Bhati v. ICAI (Rajasthan HC) — certificate of posting is not positive proof of delivery.

Analysis: Positive evidence is needed: registered A/D, hand delivery against acknowledgement, e-mail acknowledgement to the ICAI-registered/official e-mail, or UDIN route.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (8).

Q.q: CA Raja was appointed auditor of Castle Ltd. at the AGM but declined. The Board appointed CA Rani in his place, and she accepted.
Q.a:
Provision: s.139(8) — Board fills only a casual vacancy; s.139(10) — if no auditor is appointed at the AGM, the existing auditor continues. FS Part I Clause (9) — ascertain compliance with ss.139–141 before accepting.

Analysis: Non-acceptance by Raja is not a casual vacancy; the Board's appointment is invalid. Rani accepted without verifying.

Conclusion: CA Rani is guilty under Clause (9).

Q.q: Mr. X accepted appointment as statutory auditor of ABC Ltd. without communicating with the previous auditor and without ascertaining compliance with ss.139 and 140.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (8) (communication) and Clause (9) (ascertaining ss.139/140 compliance).

Conclusion: Guilty under both Clauses (8) and (9).

Q.q: Mr. P, acting as liquidator of AB & Co., charged fees as a percentage of realisation of assets.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (10) with Regulation 192(a) — a receiver or liquidator may charge a percentage of realisation or disbursement of assets.

Conclusion: Not guilty.

Q.q: A CA holding COP with four articled assistants accepts a full-time lectureship in a college and becomes a partner with his brother in a business.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (11); Reg 190A resolution — full-time lectureship (courses other than ICAI's) and business interest need specific and prior Council approval.

Analysis: Neither permission was obtained. (With four articled assistants, a full-time job is also inconsistent with full-time practice.)

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (11).

Q.q: Mr. A, a CA in practice, became executive chairman of a software company on 1 April 2024 and applied to the Council for permission on 10 April 2024.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (11) — permission must precede engagement.

Analysis: From 1 to 10 April he was engaged without permission.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (11).

Q.q: CA Moksh, a tax practitioner, is editor of a non-accountancy journal and spends about 50% of his time on it.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (11) — general permission covers editorship of professional journals only; editorship of other journals needs specific permission.

Conclusion: Without specific permission he is guilty under Clause (11).

Q.q: S, a CA in practice, gives a power of attorney to an employee CA to sign reports and financial statements on his behalf.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (12) — only a member in practice who is his partner may sign such documents on his behalf; s.26 of the Act.

Analysis: An employee CA is not a partner.

Conclusion: Guilty under FS Part I (12) and SS Part II (1) for contravening s.26.

Q.q: CA Smart, abroad, directed his assistant (a CA, not a partner) to sign and issue an urgent stock certificate for a bank after verification.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (12) — a certificate expressing a professional opinion is a 'report'; only a partner who is a member in practice may sign on his behalf.

Conclusion: Guilty. Urgency is no defence.

Q.q: Mr. C, an employee who also holds COP, recommends a lawyer to his employer; the lawyer pays him a referral fee from his professional fee.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part II Clause (2) — an employee accepting part of fees from a lawyer engaged by the employer by way of commission or gratification; applies even if he holds COP.

Conclusion: Guilty under Part II (2).
Q.trap: Referral fee is allowed only between CAs in practice (FS I(3)); not from a lawyer, and not when you are the employee.

Q.q: Mr. G, while applying for COP, left blank the columns asking about other business, though he was engaged in business.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part III Clause (2) — not supplying information called for by the Institute.

Conclusion: Guilty. (Also consider FS Part I (11) for the unpermitted business.)

Q.q: Mr. X, a paid assistant, left the firm on 31 December 2024 and did not reply to ICAI's reminders asking for the date of leaving.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part III Clause (2).

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: YKS & Co., concurrent auditor of a bank, used its influence to get a loan from the bank and failed to repay.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part IV Clause (2) — other misconduct: in the Council's opinion, bringing disrepute to the profession, whether or not related to professional work.

Conclusion: Guilty of other misconduct.

Q.q: Mr. P presented a paper at a Chamber of Commerce symposium on the leather industry and shared vital information about a client's business, believing it would help the nation compete.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clause (1) — disclosure of client information without consent or legal requirement.

Analysis: No consent, no legal requirement; good intention is irrelevant; the duty continues after the engagement.

Conclusion: Guilty under SS Part I (1).

Q.q: Mr. J, auditor of XYZ Ltd., learnt that the company had taken a ₹10 lakh loan from the Employees' Provident Fund, not recorded in the books, but ignored it in his report.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clause (5) — failing to disclose a material fact known to him that is not disclosed in the FS but is necessary to make them not misleading.

Analysis: The loan is material, contravenes rules and is unrecorded.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (5). (Clause (6) may also be cited for the misstatement.)

Q.q: A CA, as authorised representative of a company before tax authorities, submitted information and explanations that turned out to be false and misleading (prepared by management).
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clauses (5) and (6) apply where the CA is concerned with the financial statement in a professional (reporting) capacity.

Analysis: He only submitted management's statements on instructions as representative; he did not report on them.

Conclusion: Not guilty (per SM).
Q.trap: If he knew the information was false, integrity (CoE 111) would bite — the SM answer assumes no knowledge.

Q.q: CA C, statutory auditor of a daily newspaper, certified circulation figures based on the MIS report without examining the books of account.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clause (7) — due diligence.

Analysis: Paid circulation needs verification of remittances from agents, credits for unsold copies, books of account. Statistical data without cross-verification is gross negligence.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (7) (and Clause (8) could be added).

Q.q: Mr. D did not complete the audit and submit his report in time for the company to meet statutory deadlines.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clause (7).

Conclusion: Guilty — not completing work in time for statutory compliance is lack of due diligence.

Q.q: Investments of A Ltd. appeared at ₹12 lakh for two years; actual investments were ₹25,000, inflated to get a bigger bank loan. The auditor relied on management.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clauses (2), (7) and (8).

Analysis: The auditor must verify existence and valuation of investments at year-end from documentary evidence and not rely blindly on management, and did not do so for two years.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clauses (2), (7) and (8).

Q.q: A charitable institution gave its auditors M/s R & Co. ₹10 lakh to invest in specified securities. They deposited it in their own savings account and made no investment for three months.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clause (10) — keep client money in a separate bank account and use it for the intended purpose within a reasonable time.

Conclusion: Guilty on both counts.

Q.q: L, a CA in practice, does not maintain books of account for his professional earnings because his income is below the s.44AA limits.
Q.a:
Provision: Council Guidelines (Ch V) — every member in practice/firm shall maintain proper books including cash book and ledger; breach → SS Part II (1).

Analysis: The Income-tax threshold is irrelevant.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: Mr. G, a partner in a 6-partner firm, alone signed 290 tax audit reports in a financial year (corporate and non-corporate assessees).
Q.a:
Provision (as amended, Nov 2026 RTP): The limit of 60 tax audits applies to each member per financial year, in aggregate across individual and firm capacity, and cannot be distributed or shared between partners. Audits under ss.44AD, 44ADA, 44AE and revised reports are not counted.

Analysis: Mr. G signed 290 reports — far above his personal limit of 60. The firm having 6 partners does not raise his limit.

Conclusion: Mr. G is guilty of professional misconduct (contravention of Council guidelines → SS Part II (1)).
Q.trap: Your printed SM answer (firm limit 360 shared among partners → not guilty) is the OLD rule. The Nov 2026 RTP reverses it — see RTP MCQ on CA Chetan.

Q.q: Mr. C accepted the 2023-24 statutory audit of PSU Ltd., whose net worth was negative for 2022-23. Accounts show ₹15,000 tax audit fees payable to the previous auditor.
Q.a:
Provision: Council Guideline (Ch VII) — do not accept if undisputed audit fee of the previous auditor is unpaid; not applicable to a sick unit.

Analysis: Negative net worth → sick unit (assuming registered ≥ 5 years). Exception applies.

Conclusion: Not guilty.

Q.q: A is auditor of Z Ltd. (turnover ₹200 crore; audit fee ₹50 lakh). The company offers him a management consultancy assignment for ₹1 crore.
Q.a:
Provision: Council Guideline (Ch IX) — for listed/PSU/public companies with turnover ≥ ₹50 crore, other services' fees must not exceed the statutory audit fee. MCS counts as 'other work'.

Analysis: ₹1 crore > ₹50 lakh.

Conclusion: Accepting would be misconduct.

Q.q: D, tax auditor of M/s ABC, received ₹2,50,000 fees on a progressive basis for FY 2023-24; the report was signed on 25 May 2024.
Q.a:
Provision: Council Guideline (Ch X) on indebtedness; Research Committee opinion — fees recovered progressively as work is done under the engagement terms do not make the auditor indebted.

Conclusion: Not guilty.

Q.q: NFRA investigated the engagement partner of a listed SME company (FY 2016-17: revenue ₹51.77 cr, inventory ₹20.60 cr, receivables ₹14.93 cr, payables ₹13.78 cr). He was appointed after year-end and did not attend the stock count or document alternative procedures; ~100% of sales went to a party earlier disclosed as related, not identified; management refused debtor/creditor contact details and no alternative procedures or fraud-risk evaluation was done. Unmodified opinion issued. Evaluate.
Q.a:
Provisions: SA 501 (attend count or alternative procedures, else modify per SA 705); SA 550 (identify related parties); SA 505 (management refusal to allow confirmation → inquire into reasons, evaluate risks including fraud, alternative procedures). SS Part I Clauses (7), (8) and (9). NFRA's power under s.132(4) Companies Act.

Analysis: (1) Late appointment doesn't excuse — alternative procedures had to be performed and documented. (2) A party disclosed as related earlier and taking ~100% of sales called for professional scepticism. (3) Refusal of contact details is a scope limitation with fraud-risk implications — none evaluated. Opinion not backed by evidence.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clauses (7), (8) and (9); NFRA imposed penalty and debarred him for two years from audits of companies/body corporates.
Q.trap: 'Not documented = not done' is the line NFRA uses. Put it in your answer.

Q.q: P, a CA in practice providing MCS, began managing portfolios of some clients (Portfolio Management Services) in 2024.
Q.a:
Provision: s.2(2)(iv) MCS resolution — adviser/consultant to an issue is allowed, but the explanation states broking, underwriting and portfolio management are not permitted. Doing it = other occupation without permission (FS Part I (11)).

Conclusion: P is guilty.

Q.q: Mr. G, sole proprietor near Churchgate, Mumbai, opens a second office in a suburb about 80 km from the municipal limits and employs three retired Income-tax Officers to run it.
Q.a:
Provision: s.27 — each office in separate charge of a member; exemption only for same premises, same city, or within 50 km of municipal limits.

Analysis: 80 km is beyond the exemption; retired ITOs are not members.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: Write a short note on 'Other misconduct'.
Q.a:
Answer: 'Other misconduct' is defined in FS Part IV and SS Part III. It lets the Institute act on a member's conduct even when not arising from professional work, because a CA must keep the highest integrity in personal affairs too (e.g., forging a relative's will).

  • FS Part IV (1): held guilty by a civil/criminal court for an offence punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months (Board of Discipline).
  • FS Part IV (2): in the Council's opinion, brings disrepute to the profession or Institute, whether or not related to professional work.
  • SS Part III: held guilty for an offence punishable with imprisonment exceeding 6 months (Disciplinary Committee).

s.22 also preserves the Director (Discipline)'s power to inquire into conduct in any other circumstances (B. Mukherjea, SC). Conviction for moral turpitude/non-technical professional offences is also a disability under s.8(v).

Q.q: Mr. K paid 50% of his audit fees to Mr. L, a non-CA, as 'office allowance' for several years.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (2).

Analysis: Substance over nomenclature — this is sharing of fees/profits with a non-member.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: Mr. X started practice on 15 August 2024 and offered an articled assistant 1% of his firm's profits in addition to the prescribed stipend, saying she is financially weak. ICAI objects.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (2) — share of profits to anyone other than the permitted persons. (Stipend is governed by Reg 48.)

Analysis: An articled assistant is not a member or partner; the motive doesn't change the nature.

Conclusion: Guilty; ICAI's objection is valid. He may help by a higher stipend, not a profit share.

Q.q: M/s XYZ's website uses bright green, runs on 'push' technology, and displays partners' names and major clients without any regulator requirement.
Q.a:
Provision: Website guidelines under FS Part I (6).

Analysis: Colour — no restriction. Push technology — not allowed (pull only, SM position). Client names — not allowed unless required by a regulator, with the italicised note.

Conclusion: Guilty on push model and client names.
Q.trap: Exam answer follows the SM (pull only). The Code of Ethics 2026 allows push for non-exclusive services, but that is outside the Nov 2026 RTP.

Q.q: During a TV interview a partner handed the firm's bio-data (international affiliation, his achievements and recognition as a tax expert) to the anchor, who read it out.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (6); interview guidance — no publicity or attainments; facts only in answer to specific questions.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (6) (Clause (7) also relevant).

Q.q: (a) A newspaper ad with Mr. X's photograph congratulating him on his office opening. (b) Mr. X wrote several letters to the Assistant Registrar of Co-operative Societies saying though empanelled, no audit was allotted, and requested him to look into it.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (6).

(a) A prominent ad with photograph on office opening is solicitation by advertisement → guilty.

(b) Asking the reason for non-allotment is fine, but repeated letters amounting to a request for allotment are solicitation → guilty.

Conclusion: Guilty in both.

Q.q: A practising CA's visiting card says 'Chartered Accountant' and 'Cost Accountant'.
Q.a:
Provision: s.7 and FS Part I (7). Council allows letters A.C.M.A./F.C.M.A., not the designation 'Cost Accountant', and never simultaneously with 'Chartered Accountant'.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: Mr. Nigal, speaking at a Ministry of Textiles conference, called himself a management expert, said his firm offers tax and audit at reasonable rates, asked the audience to approach his firm, and handed out business cards.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clauses (6) and (7).

Analysis: 'Management expert' is not a permitted designation; promoting firm services and rates and distributing cards is solicitation. Speakers may describe themselves as CAs and give relevant qualifications, but must be objective, not promotional.

Conclusion: Guilty under both clauses.

Q.q: Mr. A (proprietor of M/s A & Co.) went abroad for 3 months, delegating routine work to Mr. Y, his CA employee. Y: (i) issued audit queries; (ii) issued a production certificate under GST law; (iii) attended income-tax proceedings as authorised representative.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (12); Council list of routine matters that may be delegated.

(i) Audit queries — delegable → no misconduct.
(ii) Production certificate — an attest document, not routine → A is guilty under Clause (12).
(iii) Routine tax matters subject to s.288 Income-tax Act — delegable → no misconduct.

Conclusion: Mr. A is guilty only for (ii).

Q.q: XYZ Ltd. applied for a bank loan. The bank calls you, the auditor, asks your opinion of the company and details of items in the FS available in your working papers. Respond.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clause (1); SA 200 (confidentiality).

Response: Do not disclose without the client's specific consent or legal requirement. Working papers are the auditor's property; extracts may be shared only with the client, at discretion. Politely decline; ask the bank to obtain information from the company or get the company's written consent.

Conclusion: Disclosure without consent = misconduct.

Q.q: A newly qualified CA sought clients through calls to family and friends, launched a colourful website, shared it on all his social media posts and tagged 30 local traders with 'Easy Online Stock Certification Services', mentioning current clients.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (6); website guidelines.

Analysis: Soliciting through personal calls; pushing the website via social media tags; catch phrase; client names; stock certification is attestation.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (6). A website itself is fine if compliant.

Q.q: Mr. D was director simplicitor of XYZ Pvt. Ltd., resigned after one year and accepted its statutory audit.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clause (4); Council decision — a member shall not accept audit of a company for two years from completion of tenure or resignation as director.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: Mr. F gave advisory, GST consultancy, a compilation engagement and ERP set-up to PQR Pvt. Ltd., later found part of a money-laundering group. Asked for company details, he says he gave only consultancy and needn't keep information.
Q.a:
Provision: ICAI KYC norms (mandatory for attestation assignments).

Analysis (SM view): For a corporate client he should hold: name, address, business description, parent company, last audited FS, type of engagement, PAN, CIN, directors' names/addresses/DINs.

Conclusion: His contention is not valid.
Q.trap: The SM applies KYC here though the services were non-attest; reproduce the SM's list and conclusion.

Q.q: Auditor Mr. S delegated to articles/staff: (i) audit queries; (ii) memorandum of cash/physical verification; (iii) letters forwarding draft FS; (iv) acknowledgements for records; (v) signing the company's financial statements.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (12) and Council's delegable list.

Analysis: (i)–(iv) are routine, delegable. (v) signing FS can be done only by a member in practice who is his partner.

Conclusion: Guilty only for (v).

Q.q: Mr. S (Chennai) does equity research and advises friends/relatives (no retail report); is a paper-setter for his old school; owns agricultural land and farms. He became an undischarged insolvent after losses, later discharged with a court certificate that insolvency was due to misfortune without misconduct.
Q.a:
(A) Equity research: ESB — may be an equity research adviser but cannot publish a retail report. No retail report → no misconduct.
(B) Paper-setter; agriculture: both under general permission (Reg 190A) → no misconduct.
(C) Insolvency: s.8(iv) bars a discharged insolvent without a misfortune certificate. He has it → no disability now.

Conclusion: No misconduct and no bar to membership.
Q.trap: During the period he was an undischarged insolvent, s.8(iii) applied — if asked, say his name could be removed for that period.

Q.q: CA Pankaj, valuer under direct taxes, charges fees as a percentage of the property value.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (10) with Reg 192(c).

Conclusion: Not guilty.

Q.q: Mr. Johny, presenting on bank audits at a seminar, used examples from his clients and shared significant client information to help the audience understand.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clause (1); CoE confidentiality.

Conclusion: Guilty — no consent, no legal requirement.

Q.q: CA Vaayu, auditor of Viva Ltd. (turnover > ₹200 crore; audit fee ₹80 lakh), accepted representation before ITAT for ₹1.75 crore.
Q.a:
Provision: Council Guideline (Ch IX) — 'other work' excludes audit under other statutes, certification by statutory auditor and representation before an authority.

Conclusion: Not guilty even though the fee exceeds the audit fee.
Q.trap: Swap 'representation' for 'MCS' and the answer becomes guilty (see Illustration 39).

Q.q: Sanjeev & Associates responded to a PF Office tender for quarterly e-TDS returns: EMD ₹7,500; open to all categories; maximum fee ₹7,500 per quarter.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (6) proviso; tender guideline.

Analysis: e-TDS filing is open to other professionals; the minimum-fee condition applies only to exclusive CA areas.

Conclusion: May respond.

Q.q: CA Shubh, an IS audit expert, became MD of ZX Ltd., a management consultancy company, without ICAI's prior permission. A friend says he loses full-time COP and can't do attest work or train articles.
Q.a:
Provision: Guidelines for corporate form of practice — a member may be MD/WTD/Manager of a company exclusively rendering MCS (name approved and registered with ICAI), keep full-time COP, do attest work in individual/firm capacity and train articles.

Conclusion: Per the SM, his action is valid and the friend is wrong.
Q.trap: Add in your answer: this holds only if ZX Ltd. is exclusively in MCS and registered with ICAI; otherwise MD needs specific permission (FS I(11)).

Q.q: CA Angad digitally signed the ROC form for a director's resignation without verifying the resignation letter, on which the director's signature had been copy-pasted by another director.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clause (7).

Analysis: Basic verification of a signature any reasonable person would do was not done; a forged resignation got filed.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: Shri Ltd., a listed company, obtained a pollution clearance by unfair means while still breaching pollution law; ₹18.75 lakh spent unlawfully was booked as pollution recycling expenditure. The Director-Finance (CA Gopal) found this on review; TCWG don't know. What should he do under NOCLAR?
Q.a:
Applicability: Section 260 applies to senior professional accountants (including directors/KMP) employed in listed entities → applies to CA Gopal.

Response steps: (1) Obtain an understanding of the matter (laws, nature, consequences). (2) Address it — discuss with his superior/management and escalate to TCWG (audit committee); seek to have it rectified, remediated and deterred; consider disclosure to authorities where required. (3) Seek advice (legal, within the organisation, the Institute). (4) Determine whether further action is needed — consider management/TCWG response; may inform the external auditor; may resign. (5) Determine whether to disclose to an appropriate authority (e.g., Pollution Control Board). (6) Imminent breach causing substantial public harm — may disclose immediately. (7) Document everything.

Also: Integrity — shouldn't be associated with FS misclassifying an unlawful payment.

Q.q: CA Kapila, filling ICAI's Multi-purpose Empanelment Form, shows income from equity F&O as business income. Any issue? What if it were currency or commodity derivatives?
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (11); ESB announcement — derivatives in personal capacity (not for clients) are allowed for equity and currency derivatives without permission; commodity derivatives are not allowed.

Conclusion: Equity F&O — no misconduct. Currency derivatives — same. Commodity derivatives — guilty under Clause (11).

Q.q: Enumerate circumstances where a PA is or might be required to disclose confidential information, and points to consider before disclosure (Subsection 114).
Q.a:
When disclosure is required/appropriate: (1) required by law — evidence in legal proceedings; disclosure of infringements to public authorities; (2) permitted by law and authorised by client/employer; (3) professional duty or right, when not prohibited by law — Peer/Quality Review of ICAI; inquiry by a professional/regulatory body; protecting the PA's interests in legal proceedings; complying with technical and professional standards including ethics.

Points to consider: (1) whether any party's interests, including third parties, could be harmed even with consent; (2) whether all relevant information is known and substantiated; (3) the proposed type of communication and to whom; (4) whether recipients are appropriate.

Q.q: CA Raj accepted appointment by the Central Government as 'Secretary' in his professional capacity for a Metro project for 2 years, not on a salary-cum-full-time basis.
Q.a:
Provision: Reg 191 — may take up a Government appointment or act as Secretary in professional capacity if not salary-cum-full-time; FS Part I (11).

Conclusion: Not guilty.

Q.q: CA R, auditor of listed TP Ltd., finds GST/Income-tax notices and child labour at the plant, follows SA 250 and says SA 250 and NOCLAR are the same. Agree?
Q.a:
No. Differences: (1) SA 250 applies only to audit; NOCLAR applies to PAs in service and in practice, including non-audit services. (2) SA 250 covers laws with direct effect and laws fundamental to operations; NOCLAR goes further to non-compliance causing substantial harm with serious financial or non-financial consequences. (3) SA 250 doesn't define stakeholders; NOCLAR focuses on investors, creditors, employees and the public. (4) Imminent-breach disclosure to an appropriate authority exists only under NOCLAR.

Also: For a listed entity with net worth ≥ ₹250 crore, Section 360 applies to CA R — he must go beyond SA 250 (understand, discuss with management/TCWG, consider disclosure to authority, document).

Q.q: CA Kumar (no assurance practice) offers to plead XYZ Ltd.'s ITAT appeal against a ₹10 crore demand for 10% of the demand reduced.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (10); Reg 192(h) — Council permitted contingent/percentage fees for non-assurance services to non-audit clients.

Conclusion: Not guilty (XYZ is not his audit client).
Q.trap: Same facts with an audit client → guilty.

Q.q: Can a CA firm register on the GeM portal to render professional services to Government departments?
Q.a:
Analysis: Listing on app-based aggregators is not permitted, and roving empanelment enquiries are not allowed. GeM is operated by the Government buyer itself — registration is a pre-requirement for serving Government departments, not an aggregator listing or roving enquiry.

Conclusion: Permitted (ICAI announcement), but bids must comply with tender guidelines.

Q.q: CA Gyan, a CA in practice and an engineer, wants to do the registered valuer course and work as registered valuer for plant and machinery under the Companies Act.
Q.a:
Analysis: Attending classes/exams is generally permitted → doing the course is fine. MCS covers Registered Valuer only for securities or financial assets; plant and machinery valuation is outside MCS.

Conclusion: He may do the course but cannot practise as a valuer of plant and machinery while in practice as a CA.

Q.q: CA Evan (proprietor, 2 years in practice) records fees in notes on his mobile and files his return from them.
Q.a:
Provision: Council Guideline — proper books including cash book and ledger; breach → SS Part II (1).

Conclusion: Guilty — phone notes are not books of account.

Q.q: CA Rahul, without COP, issued a raw-material consumption certificate as a CA in practice and applied for COP the next day.
Q.a:
Provision: s.6 (COP before practice) — contravention of the Act → SS Part II Clause (1). (s.24 also: a member without COP representing to be in practice.)

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: CA Lucky, facing a special notice that he won't be reappointed at TRIM Ltd.'s AGM, sent a representation highlighting his contributions to strengthening controls and his willingness to continue.
Q.a:
Provision: s.140(4)(iii) Companies Act gives the right to make representation; FS Part I (6) — the representation should state in a dignified manner that he acted independently and conscientiously and may state willingness to continue; no publicity or canvassing.

Analysis: Listing contributions is canvassing.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (6).

Q.q: CA Anita joined as audit executive on 1 April 2024 and ignored ICAI's reminders to state her appointment date and submit her membership certificate.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part III Clause (2).

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: CA Arun referred a client needing a GST audit to CA Bina. Bina paid Arun 10% of the fee as referral fee. Separately, Arun shared 25% of fees with a Company Secretary who jointly handled a merger assignment. Comment.
Q.a:
Provisions: FS Part I (3) — referral fees between members in practice are not prohibited. FS Part I (2) and Reg 53A — fees may be shared with members of prescribed professional bodies including ICSI.

Conclusion: Arun is not guilty on either count.

Q.q: CA Deepa, in practice, becomes a designated partner (non-working, no remuneration) in an LLP trading in garments.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (4); Council view — a member in practice cannot be partner/designated partner of an LLP not carrying on professional work; the director-simplicitor relaxation doesn't extend to LLPs. Also FS Part I (11).

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: CA Farhan is statutory auditor of S Ltd. He accepts appointment as an independent director (non-executive) of H Ltd., the holding company of S Ltd.
Q.a:
Provision: Proviso to FS Part I (11) permits director simplicitor unless he or a partner is the company's auditor. ESB clarification — the auditor of a subsidiary cannot be a director of its holding company (independence).

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: CA Gauri is a part-time lecturer at City College and accepts the audit of the college. Her partner is a trustee of the Hope Trust, whose audit the firm also accepts.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I (4); Council decisions — a CA shall not accept audit of a college where he is a part-time lecturer, or of a trust where his partner is employee or trustee.

Conclusion: Guilty on both.

Q.q: CA Harsh is statutory auditor of M Ltd. The company asks him also to be its internal auditor for a separate fee; he accepts. He is also its tax auditor.
Q.a:
Provision: s.144(b) Companies Act prohibits internal audit by the statutory auditor; Council also prohibits the statutory auditor being internal auditor of the same entity (SS Part I (4)); acting in contravention of the Companies Act → SS Part II (5).

Analysis: Tax audit by the statutory auditor is not prohibited. The internal audit is.

Conclusion: Guilty for accepting internal audit; tax audit is fine.
Q.trap: Reverse case: the internal auditor cannot be the tax auditor or GST auditor.

Q.q: CA Ishaan's wife holds shares of face value ₹1,80,000 in P Ltd.; Ishaan accepts P Ltd.'s audit. He also owes R & Co., a partnership firm whose audit he accepts, ₹1,50,000 for a car purchase.
Q.a:
Provision: s.141(3)(d)(i) with Rule 10 — a relative may hold securities of face value up to ₹1 lakh; above that the auditor is disqualified (SS Part I (4), SS Part II (5)). Council Guideline (Ch X) — non-company concern: indebtedness above ₹1,00,000 bars appointment.

Conclusion: Guilty on both counts (₹1.8 lakh > ₹1 lakh; ₹1.5 lakh > ₹1 lakh).
Q.trap: For a company, the indebtedness limit is ₹5 lakh (s.141(3)(d)(ii)); the ₹1 lakh guideline applies where the statute sets no limit.

Q.q: CA Jaya is offered the statutory audit of K Pvt. Ltd. (in business for 8 years, positive net worth). The previous auditor's audit fee of ₹2 lakh, provided in the accounts signed by both, is unpaid. She accepts, telling the client to pay later.
Q.a:
Provision: Council Guideline (Ch VII) — must not accept if the undisputed audit fee of the previous auditor for statutory audit is unpaid, unless a sick unit. Provision in accounts signed by both = undisputed.

Analysis: Not a sick unit (positive net worth).

Conclusion: Guilty (SS Part II (1) read with FS Part I (8) professional reasons).

Q.q: CA Kiran, appointed branch auditor of a nationalised bank with the audit to start in 3 days, sent a letter to the previous auditor by registered A/D, gave a conditional acceptance, and began work.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (8); Council relief for government/bank audits where time is too short — send the communication, give conditional acceptance subject to professional objections, start urgent work, decide finally after the reply.

Conclusion: Not guilty.

Q.q: CA Lata e-mailed the outgoing auditor at his e-mail address registered with ICAI and received an acknowledgement before accepting. Another letter sent by registered A/D to a different predecessor came back marked 'office found locked'.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (8) — acknowledgement via ICAI-registered e-mail is positive evidence; 'office found locked' on the A/D is deemed delivery.

Conclusion: Compliant in both cases.

Q.q: CA Mohan is a partner in firm A (3 partners) and firm B (2 partners). Firm A holds 70 company audits and firm B 55. Mohan also holds 8 company audits individually. Are the limits breached?
Q.a:
Provision: Council Guideline (Ch VIII) — 30 company audits per member; for firms, 30 per partner; a partner of several firms (and in individual capacity) is limited to 30 in aggregate.

Analysis: Firm A capacity 90 (3 × 30) — holds 70; Firm B capacity 60 (2 × 30) — holds 55. Both firms are within limits. Mohan's own count (his share of firm A and firm B audits plus 8 individual audits) must not exceed 30.

Conclusion: No breach so long as Mohan's aggregate is within 30. (The Code of Ethics 2026 raises the ceiling to 40, but that is not in the Nov 2026 RTP — write 30.)
Q.trap: OPCs and dormant companies are excluded in the SM count; head office plus branches of one company = one audit.

Q.q: CA Neel, auditor of listed N Ltd. (audit fee ₹40 lakh), takes a ₹30 lakh valuation assignment. His wife's consultancy firm, in which she is sole partner, takes a ₹25 lakh MCS assignment from N Ltd.
Q.a:
Provision: Council Guideline (Ch IX) — limit applies to the statutory auditor and associate concerns together; associate concern includes a firm where a relative is partner.

Analysis: ₹30 lakh + ₹25 lakh = ₹55 lakh > ₹40 lakh audit fee.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: CA Om received ₹5 lakh from a client in April to pay the client's advance tax due in June, kept it in his firm's current account, and paid it in September.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I (10) — money not to be spent within a reasonably short time must be kept in a separate bank account and used for its purpose within a reasonable time.

Conclusion: Guilty on both limbs.

Q.q: CA Pooja signed the audit report of a trust after her friend, a CA in employment (not practising), did the whole audit on her behalf.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I (2) — examination must be by her, her partner, her employee or another CA in practice.

Conclusion: Guilty. (An employed CA is not a CA in practice.)

Q.q: CA Ravi prepared a 5-year projected P&L for a client's bank loan and signed it with his firm name as 'certified true and correct'.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I (3) — may prepare/review forecasts if the report states sources, basis and major assumptions and does not vouch for accuracy.

Conclusion: 'Certified true and correct' vouches for accuracy → guilty. Had he reported assumptions and disclaimed accuracy, no misconduct.

Q.q: CA Sonal could not verify the existence of investments forming the company's only significant asset. Her report said: 'Subject to verification of investments, the financial statements give a true and fair view.'
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I (8) — where exceptions are so material as to negate an opinion, disclaim (SA 705).

Conclusion: Guilty — a 'subject to' opinion is wrong here.

Q.q: CA Tanvi, finance manager of V Ltd., shared V Ltd.'s product-wise margins with a friend working at a competitor.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part II (2) — employee disclosing confidential information except as required by law or permitted by employer.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: CA Uday stated in his empanelment application to ICAI that he had 10 years of practice when he had 4. Separately, he did not reply to ICAI's letter asking for details of his other occupation.
Q.a:
Provisions: False particulars knowingly given to the Institute → SS Part II (3). Not supplying information called for → FS Part III (2).

Conclusion: Guilty under both.

Q.q: CA Vikram, liquidator of a company, used ₹20 lakh from asset realisations for his personal home loan.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part II (4) — defalcation/embezzlement of money received in professional capacity; also SS Part I (10) (liquidator's money must be in separate account).

Conclusion: Guilty; heard by the Disciplinary Committee.

Q.q: CA Waqar was convicted under a law where the offence is punishable with imprisonment up to 2 years; the court imposed a fine only. CA Yash was convicted of an offence punishable with up to 3 months. Which Schedule? Who hears?
Q.a:
Provision: Classification depends on the punishment prescribed ('punishable with'), not the sentence actually imposed.

Analysis: Waqar — punishable > 6 months → SS Part III, Disciplinary Committee. Yash — ≤ 6 months → FS Part IV (1), Board of Discipline.

Conclusion: Both guilty of other misconduct; different forums and penalty ranges.

Q.q: CA Zoya sent Diwali greeting cards with 'CA Zoya, Zoya & Co., Chartered Accountants' to clients, relatives and friends, and also to 200 local shopkeepers she doesn't know.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (6); Council — designation and firm name may be used on greeting cards sent only to clients, relatives and friends.

Conclusion: Fine for clients/relatives/friends; guilty for cards to unknown shopkeepers (indirect solicitation).

Q.q: A CA firm sponsored a city marathon; its banner showed the firm name with 'Chartered Accountants'. A partner separately sponsored a CSR tree plantation as 'CA Anil'.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (6) — sponsorship of events not permitted (except approved ICAI CPE events); CSR activities may show individual name with prefix 'CA' but not firm name or CA logo.

Conclusion: Firm guilty for the marathon; CA Anil not guilty for the CSR mention.

Q.q: A CA firm published an advertisement in a newspaper for its Silver Jubilee celebration, and another ad announcing its change of office address.
Q.a:
Provision: Council permits ads for Silver/Golden/Diamond/Platinum/Centenary celebrations and bare-fact announcements of change of address.

Conclusion: Not guilty (keep the change-of-address ad to bare facts).

Q.q: CA Bhavya wrote to 50 newly incorporated companies (from ROC data) offering her services for their first audit.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (6) — roving letters/e-mails to persons likely to need a CA's services amount to advertisement.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: CA Chetan, while doing the tax work of client X introduced to him by CA Dev (X's regular auditor), accepted X's statutory audit when X approached him directly.
Q.a:
Provision: Council decision under FS Part I (6) — a member should not accept original work of a client introduced by another member; he should ask the client to come through that member.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: A CA firm's letterhead reads 'Established 1985' and lists 'Tax & Audit Specialists'. A partner's visiting card shows 'CA, Member of Parliament'.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (7); s.7 — date of establishment must not appear on letterheads; descriptive attainments are advertisement; no other designations such as MP with CA.

Conclusion: Guilty on all three.

Q.q: CA Esha's office manager (non-CA) signed and issued a net-worth certificate on her letterhead while she was hospitalised.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (12); s.26 — no person other than a member may sign documents on behalf of a CA in practice (fine ₹1–5 lakh on first conviction for the signer).

Conclusion: CA Esha is guilty under FS I (12) and SS II (1) (contravention of s.26); the manager is liable under s.26.

Q.q: CA Farah, newly employed as CFO, agreed to pay 10% of her salary for a year to the recruitment consultant's partner who 'fixed' her appointment.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part II (1) — sharing emoluments of employment with any person to procure or retain the job.

Conclusion: Guilty. (Paying a normal recruiter fee by the employer is different.)

Q.q: CA Girish, an associate, uses 'FCA' on his letterhead because he has completed 5 years in practice, though he has not applied for fellowship.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part III (1) — acting as fellow without being one; fellowship requires application and grant.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: CA Hema, statutory auditor of W Ltd., agrees to handle W Ltd.'s income-tax appeal for 5% of the tax saved.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (10); Reg 192(h) permits contingent fees only for non-assurance services to non-audit clients.

Conclusion: Guilty — W Ltd. is her audit client.

Q.q: CA Ivan charges (i) the co-operative society he audits 1% of its working capital; (ii) a client 8% of bad debts recovered; (iii) a startup 2% of funds raised.
Q.a:
Provision: Reg 192(b), (f), (e).

Conclusion: All permitted.

Q.q: CA Jatin issued 40 turnover certificates for bank loans without generating UDIN, saying they were 'just certificates'.
Q.a:
Provision: UDIN guidelines — mandatory for all certificates from 1 Feb 2019; breach of Council guidelines → SS Part II (1).

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: Firm P, part of the 'Alpha & Affiliates' network, is statutory auditor of Z Ltd. Firm Q, of the same network, accepts Z Ltd.'s internal audit. Firm R wants to join both Alpha & Affiliates and Beta & Affiliates.
Q.a:
Provision: Networking guidelines — if one network firm is statutory auditor, no network firm may take internal audit/book-keeping/prohibited services; a firm can join only one network.

Conclusion: Q is guilty; R cannot join two networks.

Q.q: CA Kavya accepted appointment as auditor of L Ltd. in place of the retiring auditor on the basis of a certificate from the company secretary that ss.139 and 140 had been complied with.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I (9) — 'ascertain' means find out for certain by verifying records (special notice, service on retiring auditor, representation circulated, resolution); a management certificate is not sufficient.

Conclusion: Guilty.

Q.q: CA Lakshmi's firm has its HO in Pune and a branch in a town 45 km beyond Pune's municipal limits, both in her charge. She attends the branch 3 days a week.
Q.a:
Provision: s.27 exemption — second office within 50 km of the municipal limits of the city of the first office may be in the same member's charge.

Conclusion: Not guilty; she must declare the main office.
Q.trap: If the branch were 55 km away, a separate member in charge (resident or attending ≥ 182 days) would be needed.

Q.q: Identify the threats: (a) audit partner's son joins the client as CFO; (b) firm designs the client's payroll system and then audits payroll; (c) client threatens to change auditors unless a provision is reversed; (d) firm represents the client in a GST dispute before the Tribunal; (e) fees from one client form 35% of a small firm's income.
Q.a:
(a) Familiarity (and self-interest) — close family member in a position to influence FS.
(b) Self-review — evaluating own work.
(c) Intimidation.
(d) Advocacy.
(e) Self-interest/intimidation (fee dependence) — below the 40% non-PIE disclosure line, but still evaluate.

For each: evaluate using the reasonable and informed third party test; eliminate, apply safeguards (different team, independent review, another firm) or decline.

Q.q: Explain the procedure after a complaint against a CA alleging both First and Second Schedule misconduct, and the appeal route.
Q.a:
1. Complaint with fee (or information) to the Director (Discipline), who forms a prima facie opinion.
2. Matter under both Schedules → Disciplinary Committee (First Schedule only → Board of Discipline).
3. If no prima facie case: placed before the Board of Discipline, which may close or direct further investigation.
4. DC enquiry with civil court powers (summons, documents, affidavits).
5. If guilty: reprimand, removal permanently or for any period, fine up to ₹5 lakh.
6. Appeal to the Appellate Authority within 90 days by the member, or by Director (Discipline) with Council authorisation; it may confirm, modify, set aside, change the penalty, remit, or pass any order after hearing.

Q.q: PNBM & Associates has four partners. Partner Chetan signed 68 tax audit reports under s.44AB (excluding audits covered by ss.44AD, 44ADA and 44AE). He argues that with 4 partners the firm's ceiling is 240, so any partner may sign more than 60 as long as the firm's total is within 240. Is he guilty?
Q.a:
RTP answer: (b) — Yes, guilty. The ceiling of 60 tax audit reports applies individually to each member, irrespective of the number of partners in the firm.

Why: Under the amended guideline the limit is an aggregate per member per financial year and cannot be distributed or shared among partners. 68 > 60.

Wrong options: firm-level pooling (a), (d) is the old rule; corporate and non-corporate audits are counted together (c).

Q.q: CA Priya is employed as CFO of Solaris Renewables Ltd. and does not hold a certificate of practice. She appeared before income-tax authorities as the company's authorised representative. A fellow employee, Karan, asks her to represent him in his personal income-tax assessment, and she agrees.
Q.a:
RTP answer: (c) — Priya may appear as tax representative of her employer, but may not represent Karan; that would be professional misconduct.

Why: Representing the employer is part of her employment. Acting as representative for costing, financial or taxation matters for anyone else is deemed practice (s.2(2), Reg 191), which requires a COP (s.6). Doing it without COP contravenes the Act → SS Part II (1).
Q.trap: Option (b) sounds kind — 'another employee of the same company'. Karan's personal assessment is not the employer's work.

Q.q: CA Anshul, statutory auditor of Rise Ltd., obtained details of significant litigation, regulatory investigations and tax disputes during the audit. The Managing Director asks him to share certain audit working papers and internal findings with the company for internal restructuring.
Q.a:
Provision: SS Part I Clause (1) — no disclosure of information acquired in the engagement to anyone other than the client, without client consent or legal requirement. Duty continues after the assignment.

Working papers vs information: Working papers are the auditor's property; the client (or other auditors of the group) has no right of access. The auditor may, at his discretion, give portions or extracts to the client. Information may be shared only with the client's consent, obtained from a competent authority — the MD if duly authorised, otherwise a Board resolution; the request must come from the client.

Conclusion (RTP): CA Anshul must not share the working papers or confidential information on the litigation, investigations or tax disputes with the MD, or anyone else, without the client's proper consent through a competent authority.
Q.trap: The requester here is the client's MD — so check whether he is authorised by the Board. The RTP answer turns on 'competent authority'.

Q.q: CA Raman holds COP and, with Bar Council permission, is also enrolled as an advocate. Appearing before the High Court in a tax matter, he files the vakalatnama as 'CA Raman, Chartered Accountant & Advocate', and uses both designations on the visiting card and letterhead for his advocacy practice.
Q.a:
Provision: FS Part I Clause (7) — no designation other than 'Chartered Accountant' on professional documents, visiting cards, letterheads or sign boards (except recognised degrees/memberships). Council: a member in practice may practise as an advocate with Bar Council permission, but must not use 'Chartered Accountant' in matters of advocacy practice, and must never use 'Chartered Accountant' and 'Advocate' simultaneously.

Analysis: He used the CA designation in an advocacy matter (vakalatnama before the High Court) and combined both titles on his card and letterhead.

Conclusion: Guilty under Clause (7) of Part I of the First Schedule.

Q.q: CA Sanjay, sole proprietor, holds 36 company audits (including 6 private companies; no OPCs or dormant companies) in FY 2026-27.
Q.a:
Exam answer (SM, not changed by the RTP): limit is 30 company audits per member → 36 > 30 → guilty (SS Part II (1)).

Add one line: the Code of Ethics 2026 (from 1 April 2026) raises the ceiling to 40, under which he would be within limits.

Also check s.141(3)(g): 20 companies, but private companies with paid-up capital below ₹100 crore, OPCs, small and dormant companies are excluded there.

Q.q: CA Uma, in practice, teaches 32 hours a week at a private coaching institute (with specific permission) and also signs tax audits.
Q.a:
Exam answer (SM): direct teaching hours may not exceed 25 a week if the member is to do attest functions → 32 > 25 → guilty under FS Part I (11).

One line extra: the Code of Ethics 2026 text states 35 hours, but that is not in the Nov 2026 RTP.

Q.q: CA Varun died on 1 June 2025. His widow completes the sale of goodwill of his proprietary firm to CA Wasim and seeks ICAI permission in August 2026.
Q.a:
Exam answer (SM): sale and ICAI permission must be completed within one year of death → about 14 months → not permissible; the firm name would not be kept in abeyance beyond one year.

One line extra: ICAI later extended the window to three years, under which it would be allowed — not part of the Nov 2026 RTP amendments.

Q.q: CA Rhea uploads tax-explainer videos on YouTube. The description shows 'CA Rhea, Partner, R & Co., Chartered Accountants', her office phone and e-mail, and a link to the firm's website.
Q.a:
Exam answer (SM): educational videos may be uploaded, but may not refer to the member's firm and may not contain contact details or website address → guilty under FS Part I (6).

One line extra: the Code of Ethics 2026 allows firm name and contact details (still not the website).

Q.q: A CA firm runs targeted e-mail and social-media campaigns pushing information about its bookkeeping and payroll outsourcing services to people who never asked for it.
Q.a:
Exam answer (SM): websites and firm information must run on a pull model; circulating information by e-mail or other modes without a specific request, or soliciting visits, is solicitation → guilty under FS Part I (6).

One line extra: the Code of Ethics 2026 permits push technology for services not exclusive to CAs (such as bookkeeping), but this is outside the Nov 2026 RTP.

Q.q: A matter involving misconduct under both Schedules is placed before:
Q.a: Answer: (b) Second Schedule or both Schedules go to the Disciplinary Committee.
Q.why: Second Schedule or both Schedules go to the Disciplinary Committee.

Q.q: The maximum period of removal from the Register the Board of Discipline can order:
Q.a: Answer: (b) BoD: up to 3 months and fine up to ₹1 lakh.
Q.why: BoD: up to 3 months and fine up to ₹1 lakh.

Q.q: Which communication is NOT positive evidence under FS Part I (8)?
Q.a: Answer: (c) J.S. Bhati — certificate of posting is not proof of delivery.
Q.why: J.S. Bhati — certificate of posting is not proof of delivery.

Q.q: Percentage fee is permitted for:
Q.a: Answer: (c) Reg 192(c).
opts: Tax representation for an audit client

Q.q: Which activity is under GENERAL permission for a member in practice?
Q.a: Answer: (c) Agriculture is generally permitted (from 9 Aug 2008); others need specific permission.
Q.why: Agriculture is generally permitted (from 9 Aug 2008); others need specific permission.

Q.q: 'Substantial interest' in a company for the Regulations means holding at least:
Q.a: Answer: (b) ≥ 20% voting power (non-fixed dividend shares) by member and/or relatives.
Q.why: ≥ 20% voting power (non-fixed dividend shares) by member and/or relatives.

Q.q: A 'sick unit' for the undisputed-fee guideline is one registered for at least ___ years with accumulated losses ≥ net worth.
Q.a: Answer: (b) Five years.

Q.q: Which is excluded from 'other work' in the non-audit fee ceiling?
Q.a: Answer: (c) Excluded: audit under other statutes, certification by statutory auditor, representation.
Q.why: Excluded: audit under other statutes, certification by statutory auditor, representation.

Q.q: A network name must end with:
Q.a: Answer: (c) '& Affiliates'.

Q.q: NOCLAR for PAs in public practice (per SM) applies to audits of listed entities with net worth of at least:
Q.a: Answer: (b) Listed in India and net worth ≥ ₹250 crore.
Q.why: Listed in India and net worth ≥ ₹250 crore.

Q.q: Conviction for an offence punishable with imprisonment of 5 months falls under:
Q.a: Answer: (a) Not exceeding 6 months → FS Part IV (1).
Q.why: Not exceeding 6 months → FS Part IV (1).

Q.q: Second office without a separate member in charge is allowed if it is within ___ of the municipal limits of the city of the first office:
Q.a: Answer: (b) 50 km.

Q.q: Which cannot be delegated to a non-partner?
Q.a: Answer: (c) Certificates express an opinion — FS Part I (12).
Q.why: Certificates express an opinion — FS Part I (12).

Q.q: For the Nov 2026 exam (SM, unchanged by the RTP), the ICAI ceiling on company audits per partner is:
Q.a: Answer: (b) 30 per partner, including private companies, excluding OPCs and dormant companies. (20 is the Companies Act limit; 40 is the Code of Ethics 2026 figure, outside the exam cut-off.)
Q.why: 30 per partner, including private companies, excluding OPCs and dormant companies. (20 is the Companies Act limit; 40 is the Code of Ethics 2026 figure, outside the exam cut-off.)

Q.q: Which tax audit is NOT counted towards the limit of 60 (Nov 2026 RTP)?
Q.a: Answer: (c) Revised reports and audits under s.44AB(c)/(d)/(e) for ss.44AE/44ADA/44AD persons are excluded; everything else counts towards the member's personal 60.
opts: Tax audit of a firm signed in individual capacity
Tax audit signed as partner of a second firm
Q.why: Revised reports and audits under s.44AB(c)/(d)/(e) for ss.44AE/44ADA/44AD persons are excluded; everything else counts towards the member's personal 60.

Q.q: Fee-dependence disclosure to ICAI for a PIE audit client is required when fees exceed ___ of firm fees for two consecutive years:
Q.a: Answer: (b) PIE 20%, non-PIE 40%; firms with total fees ≤ ₹20 lakh exempt.
Q.why: PIE 20%, non-PIE 40%; firms with total fees ≤ ₹20 lakh exempt.

Q.q: An appeal against a DC order must be filed within:
Q.a: Answer: (c) 90 days from communication of the order.
Q.why: 90 days from communication of the order.

Q.q: CA Ravi discovers that a return he helped prepare and which the client has already filed contains a materially misleading statement that the client supplied negligently. Ravi issues a modified report. Has he breached the fundamental principle of integrity? What else must he do?
Q.a:
Provision: Code of Ethics, Subsection 111 (integrity): a professional accountant shall not knowingly be associated with reports or returns containing materially false or misleading statements, including statements provided negligently, or that omit or obscure required information.

Analysis: The statement was materially misleading, so association is the concern. The Code says there is no breach if a modified report is issued, and that once aware of the association the accountant must take steps to be disassociated.

Conclusion: Ravi is not in breach by issuing the modified report, but he must still take steps to disassociate himself from the misleading return.
Q.trap: Stopping at "modified report, so no breach". The duty to take steps to be disassociated continues.

Q.q: A member's name was removed from the Register on 15 June 2025 for non-payment of the prescribed fee. On 20 September 2025 (same year) he applies for restoration and pays the arrears. (a) What must he pay? (b) From which date is his membership restored? (c) Would the answer differ if he applied in 2026?
Q.a:
Provision: Section 20 of the CA Act, 1949 read with Regulation 19.

(a) A member removed for non-payment may be re-entered on paying the arrears of the annual fee, entrance fee and additional fee.

(b) Where the application and fees are received in the same year of removal, restoration is from the date of removal (15 June 2025).

(c) In other cases restoration is from the date the application and fee are received. Where removal was under an order of the Board of Discipline, Disciplinary Committee, Appellate Authority or High Court, restoration follows that order.
Q.trap: Treating the restoration date as always the date of payment.

Q.q: CA Sunil engages Mr Kapoor, who is neither his employee nor his partner, to approach companies and obtain audit appointments for Sunil's firm. Separately, a salaried employee of Sunil telephones listed companies and offers the firm's audit services. Comment.
Q.a:
Provision: First Schedule, Part I, Clause (5): a CA is guilty if he secures professional business through a person who is not his employee or partner, or by means not open to a chartered accountant. Acts of employees to secure work are themselves subject to Clauses (6) and (7).

Analysis: Mr Kapoor is neither employee nor partner, and the proviso covers only arrangements allowed under Clauses (2), (3) and (4). The employee's telephone solicitation is soliciting under Clause (6).

Conclusion: Sunil is guilty of professional misconduct under Clause (5) of Part I of the First Schedule, and the solicitation also engages Clause (6).
Q.trap: Citing only Clause (6). Using a non-employee to get work is Clause (5).

Q.q: A CA firm with 6 partners responds to a tender and states that it has 12 partners, knowing the figure is false. In its website write-up the same firm mistakenly prints "6 partners" as "9 partners" because of a typing error; nobody at the firm noticed. Comment on each.
Q.a:
Provision: First Schedule, Part III, Clause (3): a member is guilty if, while inviting work from another CA, responding to tenders or enquiries, or advertising through a write-up, he gives information knowing it to be false.

Analysis: (a) The tender statement was made knowing it was false, so the clause applies. (b) The typing error was unnoticed and not made knowingly, so the knowledge element is missing.

Conclusion: Partly: guilty under Clause (3) of Part III of the First Schedule for the tender; not guilty on the write-up error, though the firm should correct it promptly.
Q.trap: Treating every wrong figure as misconduct. The clause needs knowledge of falsity.

Q.q: The Council has directed that members should not accept appointment as auditor of X Ltd because the earlier auditor was removed unjustifiably. CA Rao reads the earlier auditor's statement of reasons filed with the Institute, is unconvinced by it, and accepts the appointment. Comment.
Q.a:
Provision: Council guideline (Chapter XI): an incoming auditor shall follow a direction of the Council or an appropriate Committee not to accept the appointment where the earlier auditor was removed unjustifiably. Breach of a Council guideline is misconduct under Clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule.

Analysis: A direction exists. The incoming auditor may obtain and consider the statement of reasons through the Ethical Standards Board procedure, but the direction binds him whatever his personal view of the reasons.

Conclusion: CA Rao is guilty under Clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule.
Q.trap: Thinking the incoming auditor may override the direction after reading the statement of reasons.

Q.q: A firm uses the CA India logo exactly as published on a white background on its letterhead. On its visiting cards it uses a modified logo with the firm's own monogram placed inside it, rotated slightly. Comment.
Q.a:
Provision: Council logo guidelines (Chapter XVI): members may use the CA India logo as published; no alteration of font, colour, spacing or proportion; no rotation or distortion; firm logos or monograms of any kind are prohibited. A breach is misconduct through Clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule.

Analysis: The letterhead use is as published, so it is permitted. The visiting-card version alters the logo, rotates it and adds a monogram.

Conclusion: Partly: not guilty for the letterhead; guilty for the visiting cards under Clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule.
Q.trap: Treating a firm monogram as harmless branding. Firm logos and monograms of any kind are prohibited.

method: Name the exact clause: 'As per Clause (x) of Part y of the First/Second Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, a chartered accountant in practice shall be deemed to be guilty of professional misconduct if he…'. Quote the operative words of the clause. Add the Council guideline, Regulation or section it links to.

Restate only the facts that trigger or escape the clause. Apply each ingredient: who (in practice / in service / member generally), what act, any exception (proviso, Regulation 192, general permission, s.27 50 km, sick unit). One fact, one reason.

Start with 'Conclusion:' and give a clear verdict naming the clause again: 'Hence, CA X is guilty of professional misconduct under Clause (x) of Part y of the ___ Schedule.' Where parts differ, give a verdict per part.

Four-mark answers usually carry 1 mark provision, 2 marks analysis, 1 mark conclusion. Heading each paragraph helps the examiner find marks. Write the figure that is examinable for this attempt (the SM figure unless the RTP changes it) and add one line on the Code of Ethics 2026 figure where it differs.
changes: 1. FS Part I Clause (9) wording: 'sections 139 to 141 of the Companies Act, 2013 or any other law pertaining to appointment of auditors' (FS I(9)).
2. SS Part II Clause (5) inserted: acting as auditor of a company in contravention of the Companies Act, 2013 (SS II(5)).

3. Tax audit limit (replaces SM Chapter VI): 60 per member per financial year, aggregate of individual and firm capacity, cannot be shared among partners, excludes s.44AD/44ADA/44AE audits, revised reports not counted (GL: Tax audit limit). SM Illustration 37's answer becomes guilty.

Not in the RTP, so keep SM figures: company audit ceiling 30 (GL: Company audit limit); teaching 25 hours a week (FS I(11)); goodwill sale within 1 year (FS I(2)); websites pull-only (Adv: Website); educational-video rule (FS I(6)); write-up conditions (Adv: Write-up); non-audit fee trigger ₹50 crore (GL: Non-audit fee ceiling); indebtedness ₹1 lakh (GL: Indebtedness).

Code of Ethics 2026 (applicable 1 April 2026) changed several of those numbers (40 audits, 35 hours, 3 years, push for non-exclusive services, new MCS items). They are current practice but outside your exam cut-off; at most, add one line after an SM-based answer.
